extracted.intended_audience: federal agencies, regulated parties, stakeholders, and members of the public interested in federal rulemaking and information collection review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for agency rulemaking, OIRA review, and information-collection (PRA/ICR) processes, including how to prepare, evaluate, and comment on proposed regulatory actions and information collections. Covers procedural requirements, analytic expectations (cost-benefit), disclosure, and public-participation mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA notice-and-comment requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrative Procedure Act (APA) generally requires agencies to provide public notice and seek comment prior to enacting new regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal agencies must publish proposed rules in the Federal Register, solicit public comment, consider those comments, and (when issuing a final rule) describe and respond to the public comments received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency obligation to describe and respond to comments
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing a final rule, the agency must describe and respond to the public comments it received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final rules published in the Federal Register should include the agency's explanations of how public feedback was considered and what changes were made as a result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 12866 cost-benefit and reasoned-determination principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Order 12866 requires agencies to analyze costs and benefits and to, to the extent permitted by law, act only upon a reasoned determination that the benefits justify the costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For significant regulatory actions, agencies must provide an explanation of the need for the action and an assessment of potential costs and benefits; analysis should inform whether the rule is justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "significant" regulatory action
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Executive Order 12866, "significant" actions are those that meet criteria such as having an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more, creating serious inconsistency with other agencies, materially altering budgetary impacts, or raising novel legal/policy issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant regulatory actions are subject to OIRA review; OIRA designates ~500–700 actions as significant each year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "economically significant" regulatory action
rubrics_metrics.description: Economically significant regulatory actions are those likely to have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more or that adversely affect the economy, a sector, competition, jobs, environment, public health/safety, or governments/communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economically significant rules require a more detailed quantified assessment of benefits and costs and a similar analysis of potentially effective and reasonably feasible alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA review purpose and coordination role
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA coordinates interagency Executive Branch review of significant regulations to ensure compliance with Executive Order 12866 principles, incorporation of public comment, consideration of alternatives, and analysis of costs and benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA review promotes interagency coordination to avoid inconsistent, incompatible, or duplicative policies and helps ensure agencies consider consequences before proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA review time limits and extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The OIRA review period is limited by Executive Order 12866 to 90 days; there is no minimum. The review may be extended indefinitely by the head of the rulemaking agency or, on a one-time basis, by the OMB Director for up to 30 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should plan regulatory timelines with these limits in mind and be aware that indefinite extensions by the agency head are possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA return letter grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA may return a rule to the agency for reconsideration if the rule is not compatible with the law, the agency's analysis is inadequate, the regulation is not justified by the analysis, it is inconsistent with EO 12866 or Presidential priorities, or it conflicts with other Executive Branch regulations or efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A return explains why further consideration would benefit the rulemaking; it does not necessarily indicate opposition to the draft rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency withdrawal during review
rubrics_metrics.description: At any time during OIRA review, an agency may withdraw its rule from review and choose not to move forward or to resubmit it after further consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interested parties may contact the agency directly with questions regarding specific withdrawals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory analysis purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory analysis helps agencies anticipate and evaluate likely consequences of rules (both costs and benefits) and organizes evidence on key effects of various alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purposes include determining whether benefits justify costs, promoting accountability, and identifying which alternative produces the highest net benefits; careful analysis can show that less or more stringent alternatives are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB Circular A-4 and technical guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB provides guidance on best practices for regulatory analysis; the latest comprehensive guidance is OMB Circular A-4, 'Regulatory Analysis' (2003).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circular A-4 defines good regulatory analysis and standardizes measurement and reporting of benefits and costs; OMB subjected a draft to peer review and public comment before finalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 13563 principles for regulatory decisionmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Order 13563 elaborates principles including promoting public participation, reducing redundant/inconsistent requirements, considering flexible approaches, promoting scientific integrity, and conducting retrospective analysis of significant regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should: (1) engage stakeholders and make documents available for comment; (2) attempt to harmonize rules across agencies; (3) consider less burdensome/flexible tools; (4) promote scientific integrity; and (5) plan retrospective reviews of existing significant regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft documents during OIRA review are deliberative and non-public
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft documents under OIRA review are considered deliberative and are not available for public release during review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain documents exchanged between OIRA and the rulemaking agency will be made public after a regulatory action is published in the Federal Register and OIRA's review is completed.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA disclosure of meetings and materials with outside parties
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA makes public all substantive communications with parties outside the Executive Branch concerning regulatory actions under review, including subject, date, participants of meetings, and written materials received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meeting logs are kept and available on Reginfo.gov; any written materials received on rules under review are placed on the OIRA website.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best way for outside parties to influence rules under review
rubrics_metrics.description: The best way to participate is to submit comments directly to the agency during the proposed rule stage; parties may also submit comments via regulations.gov, provide written comments to the OIRA Administrator, or request meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To request a meeting with OIRA about a rule under review, use the EO 12866 Meeting Request page. Submitting through the agency at the proposed rule stage is emphasized as most effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reginfo.gov vs Regulations.gov roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Reginfo.gov displays regulatory actions and information collections currently at OIRA for review (status, length of review, economic significance), while Regulations.gov is the government-wide portal to review and comment on published regulatory actions and view supporting materials provided by agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Reginfo.gov to track OIRA-reviewed actions and Regulations.gov to submit public comments on published proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: RIN (Regulation Identifier Number) usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A RIN is assigned to identify each regulatory action listed in the Unified Agenda; agencies are asked to include RINs in Rule and Proposed Rule headings in the Federal Register to track publication history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including RINs makes it easier for the public and officials to follow an action's development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) public-comment and OMB review requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The PRA requires agencies to seek public comment on proposed information collections and to submit proposed collections for OMB review and approval before requiring or requesting information from the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRA goals include minimizing paperwork burden and ensuring maximum utility of collected information; OIRA within OMB carries out information-collection review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "information" under the PRA
rubrics_metrics.description: The PRA defines 'information' broadly to include any statement or estimate of fact or opinion in any form (numerical, graphic, narrative), whether oral or written, and includes forms, written reports, surveys, recordkeeping requirements, and third-party disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PRA applies when identical questions or reporting/recordkeeping requirements are imposed on ten or more persons (individuals, businesses, or governmental units). Applies to voluntary and mandatory collections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Collection Request (ICR) purpose and contents
rubrics_metrics.description: An ICR is an agency request for OMB approval of an information collection and includes a description of the collection, planned use, demonstration that PRA requirements are met, and may include instruments and supporting documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICRs support OMB's determination that collections are necessary and meet PRA requirements; ICRs related to proposed rules may be held until the rule is published.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICR review process (60-day and 30-day Federal Register notices)
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency publishes an initial Federal Register notice giving the public 60 days to comment on a proposed information collection, considers comments and revises as appropriate, then submits the ICR to OMB and publishes a second notice giving the public an additional 30 days to comment during OMB review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under some circumstances, agencies can request 'emergency' review with an explanation of why normal process would cause harm or is impossible; agencies must take practicable steps to consult with the public even in emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA actions on ICRs
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA may take the following actions on agency ICRs: Approval, Improperly Submitted, Withdrawn, and Disapproval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA can approve collections for up to three years and may approve with or without change. If OIRA disapproves an ICR, the agency may not proceed and no person shall be subject to penalty for failing to comply with the collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria OMB evaluates during ICR review
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB evaluates whether the information collection is necessary for the proper performance of agency functions (practical utility), minimizes Federal information-collection burden (especially on those most adversely affected), and maximizes the practical utility and public benefit of information collected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA also reviews consistency with applicable laws, regulations, and policies related to privacy, confidentiality, security, information quality, and statistical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to participate in the ICR review process and submit comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the public are encouraged to monitor Federal Register notices on information collections and provide feedback; comments can also be submitted to sponsoring agencies or to OIRA during the first 30 days of ICR review via Reginfo.gov's 'Comment' button.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A list of ICRs open for public comment is available on the Information Collection Review page and the ICR Dashboard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential Business Information (CBI) submission restriction on Reginfo.gov
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not submit information whose disclosure is restricted by statute (e.g., trade secrets, commercial or financial information) to Reginfo.gov; comments submitted through Reginfo.gov cannot be claimed as CBI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments submitted through Reginfo.gov waive any CBI claims for information submitted; use other channels if you must protect CBI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public handling, disclosure, and privacy of comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments submitted to Reginfo.gov are maintained in ROCIS. Personally identifiable information included in comments or attachments may be provided to OIRA and may be publicly disclosed on Reginfo.gov. Comments submitted online will not be publicly disclosed until OIRA concludes review; only comments verified by OIRA will be disclosed when review is completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By providing comments through Reginfo.gov, commenters consent to their use and consideration. Contact OIRA directly to verify receipt; contact info and privacy policy available on site.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICR Dashboard categories (types of ICRs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ICR Dashboard displays seven types of information collection requests: New collection, Revision, Extension without change, Reinstatement without change, Reinstatement with change, Existing collection in use without OMB Control Number, and Discontinue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: e.g., 'Revision' = substantive revision to a currently approved collection; 'Extension without change' = extend approval at least every three years via Federal Register notice; 'Discontinue' = agency requests OMB discontinue approval when collection no longer necessary. Non-material changes may be treated as technical and not require public comment.
